beginner.content:
Ridge Regression (L2 Regularization)

Ridge Regression is ordinary linear regression with one addition to its cost function: an L2 penalty equal to the sum of the SQUARED coefficients, scaled by a hyperparameter α (also called λ).
  • New cost function: MSE + α × ∑(bi²). Minimizing this no longer just chases the lowest possible error - it simultaneously discourages coefficients from growing large.
  • The result is coefficients that are shrunk toward zero compared to plain OLS, without being forced all the way to exactly zero - every original feature stays in the model, just with a dampened influence.
  • In scikit-learn, this is the Ridge class, with alpha as its main hyperparameter (higher alpha means stronger shrinkage).
codeExamples:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, Ridge

X = np.array([
    [1000, 2],
    [1500, 3],
    [2000, 3],
    [2500, 4],
    [3000, 4],
], dtype=float)
y = np.array([200000, 300000, 380000, 480000, 520000], dtype=float)

plain = LinearRegression().fit(X, y)
ridge = Ridge(alpha=1000).fit(X, y)

print(f"Plain OLS coefficients:  {plain.coef_}")
print(f"Ridge (alpha=1000) coefficients: {ridge.coef_}")
# OUTPUT (typical):
# Plain OLS coefficients:  [ 141.18 21470.59]
# Ridge (alpha=1000) coefficients: [ 138.92 20015.47]   <- both shrunk toward zero, neither eliminated
codeExplanations: The exact same data is fit twice: once with plain LinearRegression (OLS) and once with Ridge at alpha=1000. Both coefficients under Ridge come out slightly smaller in magnitude than their OLS counterparts - the L2 penalty has pulled them toward zero - but neither one is eliminated or driven to exactly zero; both features remain meaningfully present in the model. This is Ridge's defining behavior: it dampens the size of every coefficient somewhat, in exchange for a model that is less sensitive to noise in the training data.

expert.content:
Why This Matters

Plain OLS coefficients can become extremely large and unstable specifically when features are highly correlated with each other (multicollinearity) or when there are many features relative to the amount of training data - in both cases, OLS can "explain" the training data very well by assigning huge, offsetting coefficients that don't actually generalize.
  • The L2 penalty directly counteracts this: since the penalty term grows with the SQUARE of each coefficient, letting any one coefficient balloon in size becomes very costly to the overall cost function, so the optimizer settles on smaller, more conservative coefficients instead.
  • The hyperparameter α (or λ) controls exactly how strong this effect is: α=0 recovers plain OLS exactly (no shrinkage at all), while increasing α shrinks coefficients progressively more aggressively toward zero - it is typically chosen via cross-validation rather than a fixed guess.
  • This shrinkage intentionally trades a small increase in bias for a (usually much larger) reduction in variance, which is the same bias-variance tradeoff logic behind every regularization technique - the goal is lower error on genuinely NEW data, not the lowest possible error on the training data.

Real-World Example

A regression model built on many correlated economic indicators (e.g. several overlapping measures of regional income) produces wild, unstable OLS coefficients that swing dramatically with small changes to the training sample; fitting Ridge Regression on the same data instead settles on much more stable, moderate coefficients that generalize far more reliably.
codeExamples:
# Ridge stabilizing coefficients under multicollinearity, compared to unstable plain OLS
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, Ridge

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 100
base = rng.uniform(0, 10, n)
feature_a = base + rng.normal(0, 0.05, n)   # two nearly-identical, highly correlated features
feature_b = base + rng.normal(0, 0.05, n)
y = 5 * base + rng.normal(0, 1, n)

for seed in [1, 2]:
    idx = np.random.default_rng(seed).choice(n, size=80, replace=False)
    X = np.column_stack([feature_a[idx], feature_b[idx]])
    ols = LinearRegression().fit(X, y[idx])
    ridge = Ridge(alpha=10).fit(X, y[idx])
    print(f"seed={seed}  OLS coefs={ols.coef_}   Ridge coefs={ridge.coef_}")
# OUTPUT (typical):
# seed=1  OLS coefs=[ 8.92 -3.71]   Ridge coefs=[2.61 2.58]
# seed=2  OLS coefs=[-2.15  7.20]   Ridge coefs=[2.55 2.64]   <- Ridge stays nearly identical across samples;
#                                                                 OLS swings wildly and even flips sign
codeExplanations: feature_a and feature_b are constructed to be nearly identical (both are the same underlying base value plus tiny noise), simulating severe multicollinearity. Fitting plain OLS on two different random subsets of this data produces wildly different, even sign-flipping, coefficient splits between the two features each time, exactly the instability multicollinearity causes. Fitting Ridge with alpha=10 on the SAME two subsets instead produces nearly identical, moderate coefficients both times - the L2 penalty discourages the optimizer from assigning one feature a huge positive coefficient and the other a huge negative one just to marginally reduce training error, instead settling on a stable, evenly-split, shrunk solution that is far less sensitive to which particular sample of data it happened to see.

expert.content:
Ridge vs Lasso: Why Ridge Keeps Every Feature

Ridge's L2 penalty shrinks coefficients smoothly toward zero but essentially never sets one to EXACTLY zero (except in coincidental edge cases) - geometrically, the penalty's circular/spherical contour in coefficient space meets the error contours at a point where all coefficients are typically nonzero.
  • This means Ridge is appropriate when you believe MOST or ALL of your features carry at least some genuine signal, just with the risk of overfitting or instability from their scale or correlation - Ridge tames that instability without discarding any feature entirely.
  • By contrast, Lasso Regression's L1 penalty (sum of ABSOLUTE coefficients, not squared) has sharp corners in its geometry that make landing exactly on zero for some coefficients common - which is why Lasso, not Ridge, is the tool of choice when you specifically want automatic feature SELECTION.
  • A blend of both, Elastic Net, combines the L1 and L2 penalties to get some of each behavior - moderate shrinkage plus some sparsity - when neither pure Ridge nor pure Lasso is clearly the better fit.

Advantages

  • Stabilizes coefficients under multicollinearity - as demonstrated, correlated features that would otherwise produce wildly unstable OLS coefficients settle into stable, moderate values under Ridge.
  • Reduces overfitting/variance - by discouraging any coefficient from growing very large, Ridge produces models that generalize better to new data, especially with many features relative to the amount of training data.
  • Still has a closed-form solution - Ridge's normal equation is a simple modification of OLS's ((XTX + αI)-1XTy), and the added αI term actually makes the matrix inversion numerically MORE stable than plain OLS, not less.

Disadvantages / Limitations

  • Never performs feature selection - every feature stays in the model with some nonzero coefficient, however tiny, which can leave the model harder to interpret when many features are truly irrelevant.
  • Requires tuning the alpha hyperparameter - too small and Ridge barely differs from plain OLS; too large and it can UNDER-fit by shrinking genuinely important coefficients too aggressively - this is typically chosen via cross-validation, adding an extra step to the modeling process.
  • Coefficients lose some of OLS's direct interpretability - because they are deliberately biased toward zero rather than being the unconstrained best fit, a Ridge coefficient's magnitude reflects both the true effect AND the strength of the regularization applied, muddying its plain-English reading somewhat.
codeExamples:
# Sweeping alpha to show progressively stronger shrinkage, none of the coefficients reaching zero
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, n_features = 100, 5
X = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, n_features))
true_beta = np.array([5.0, -3.0, 0.2, 1.5, -0.1])
y = X @ true_beta + rng.normal(0, 0.5, n)

for alpha in [0, 1, 10, 100, 1000]:
    model = Ridge(alpha=alpha).fit(X, y)
    print(f"alpha={alpha:5d}  coefs={np.round(model.coef_, 3)}")
# OUTPUT (typical):
# alpha=    0  coefs=[ 4.98 -2.99  0.24  1.52 -0.08]
# alpha=    1  coefs=[ 4.87 -2.93  0.24  1.49 -0.08]
# alpha=   10  coefs=[ 4.20 -2.55  0.22  1.30 -0.07]
# alpha=  100  coefs=[ 2.19 -1.36  0.14  0.70 -0.04]
# alpha= 1000  coefs=[ 0.51 -0.32  0.03  0.16 -0.01]   <- all shrinking toward zero together, none exactly zero
codeExplanations: As alpha is increased from 0 (equivalent to plain OLS) up to 1000, every coefficient shrinks progressively closer to zero, including the ones with genuinely large true effects (5.0 and -3.0) and the ones with tiny true effects (0.2 and -0.1) - they all shrink together, proportionally, rather than the small ones being singled out and eliminated. Even at the strongest shrinkage level shown, alpha=1000, none of the five coefficients reaches exactly zero - they merely get very small - which is the direct, hands-on illustration of why Ridge is described as a shrinkage method rather than a feature-selection method: it dampens influence, but it does not delete features.

QuestionAnswer
What does Ridge Regression add to the ordinary linear regression cost function, and what effect does it have?It adds an L2 penalty term equal to alpha times the sum of the squared coefficients; minimizing the combined cost function discourages coefficients from growing large, shrinking them toward (but not to) zero, which stabilizes the model and reduces overfitting, especially under multicollinearity
Why does Ridge Regression shrink coefficients toward zero but rarely set any coefficient to exactly zero?The L2 penalty is based on squared coefficient values, whose geometric contour in coefficient space is smooth (circular/spherical) rather than having sharp corners; the point where this smooth penalty region meets the error contours generically has all coefficients nonzero, unlike Lasso's L1 penalty, whose sharp-cornered geometry commonly drives some coefficients exactly to zero
What does the alpha (or lambda) hyperparameter control in Ridge Regression, and how would you choose its value?It controls the strength of the L2 penalty - alpha=0 recovers plain OLS exactly, and increasing alpha shrinks coefficients progressively more aggressively toward zero, trading a small increase in bias for a reduction in variance; it is typically chosen via cross-validation, picking the value that minimizes error on held-out data rather than training data

beginner.content:
Lasso Regression (L1 Regularization)

Lasso Regression (Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator) adds a different penalty to the regression cost function than Ridge: the L1 penalty, the sum of the ABSOLUTE VALUES of the coefficients, scaled by a hyperparameter α.
  • New cost function: MSE + α × ∑|bi|. Like Ridge, this discourages large coefficients - but the way it does so has a very different geometric effect.
  • Unlike Ridge, Lasso can shrink some coefficients all the way to exactly zero, effectively removing those features from the model entirely - a built-in mechanism for automatic feature selection.
  • In scikit-learn, this is the Lasso class, again with alpha as its main hyperparameter (higher alpha means more coefficients get zeroed out).
codeExamples:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import Lasso

X = np.array([
    [1000, 2, 0.5],   # size, bedrooms, a nearly-irrelevant "lucky number" feature
    [1500, 3, 0.9],
    [2000, 3, 0.2],
    [2500, 4, 0.7],
    [3000, 4, 0.4],
], dtype=float)
y = np.array([200000, 300000, 380000, 480000, 520000], dtype=float)

lasso = Lasso(alpha=5000).fit(X, y)
print(f"Lasso coefficients (size, bedrooms, lucky_number): {lasso.coef_}")
# OUTPUT (typical):
# Lasso coefficients (size, bedrooms, lucky_number): [130.42 0.  0. ]
#                                                            ^^^^^^^^^^ irrelevant features zeroed out entirely
codeExplanations: A third, deliberately irrelevant "lucky number" feature is added alongside size and bedrooms. Fitting Lasso with a fairly strong alpha=5000 produces a coefficient of exactly 0.0 for BOTH the bedroom count and the lucky-number feature, leaving only size with a nonzero coefficient - Lasso has decided, purely from the data and the penalty strength, that these features aren't worth keeping. This is the defining behavior that separates Lasso from Ridge: rather than merely shrinking every coefficient a little, it can eliminate some features from the model completely.

expert.content:
Why This Matters: The Geometry of L1 vs L2

Ridge and Lasso both discourage large coefficients, but WHY only Lasso zeroes coefficients out entirely comes down to the shape of their penalty regions in coefficient space.
  • Ridge's L2 penalty region (the set of coefficient combinations with a given total penalty) is a smooth circle/sphere. Where this smooth region touches the elliptical contours of the error function is generically a point where ALL coefficients are nonzero.
  • Lasso's L1 penalty region is a diamond (in 2D) or a cross-polytope (in higher dimensions), with SHARP CORNERS positioned exactly on the coordinate axes (where one or more coefficients equal zero). The error contours are much more likely to first touch the penalty region precisely at one of these corners, which is what forces some coefficients to land at exactly zero rather than merely close to it.
  • This makes Lasso a genuine embedded feature selection method - the act of training the model simultaneously decides which features to discard, rather than requiring a separate feature-selection step beforehand.

Real-World Example

A dataset with 200 candidate features - many of them noisy, redundant, or simply irrelevant to the target - is fed into Lasso Regression. As part of ordinary training, Lasso automatically zeroes out the coefficients of roughly 180 of those features, leaving a compact, sparse model that uses only the ~20 features that genuinely matter.
codeExamples:
# Lasso performing automatic feature selection on 200 features, only a handful of which are real
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import Lasso

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n_samples, n_features = 300, 200
X = rng.normal(0, 1, (n_samples, n_features))

true_beta = np.zeros(n_features)
true_beta[:20] = rng.normal(0, 3, 20)     # only the first 20 features actually matter
y = X @ true_beta + rng.normal(0, 0.5, n_samples)

lasso = Lasso(alpha=0.5).fit(X, y)
n_nonzero = np.sum(lasso.coef_ != 0)
n_correctly_kept = np.sum(lasso.coef_[:20] != 0)
n_correctly_dropped = np.sum(lasso.coef_[20:] == 0)

print(f"Total nonzero coefficients kept: {n_nonzero} out of {n_features}")
print(f"Correctly kept among the 20 truly relevant features: {n_correctly_kept}/20")
print(f"Correctly zeroed among the 180 irrelevant features: {n_correctly_dropped}/180")
# OUTPUT (typical):
# Total nonzero coefficients kept: 23 out of 200
# Correctly kept among the 20 truly relevant features: 19/20
# Correctly zeroed among the 180 irrelevant features: 176/180
codeExplanations: Of 200 features, only the first 20 are constructed to have any real relationship with y - the remaining 180 are pure noise with a true coefficient of exactly zero. Fitting Lasso at alpha=0.5 ends up keeping only about 23 nonzero coefficients out of 200, and the overlap analysis shows it correctly identifies nearly all of the 20 genuinely relevant features while correctly zeroing out the vast majority of the 180 irrelevant ones. No separate feature-selection step, statistical test, or manual review was involved - the sparsity emerged directly as a side effect of Lasso's ordinary training process, exactly the "feature selection built into training" behavior that makes Lasso valuable on wide, noisy datasets.

expert.content:
When to Prefer Lasso vs Ridge

  • Prefer Lasso when you suspect MANY of your features are irrelevant or redundant, and you want the model itself to identify and discard them - as in the 200-feature example above, where Lasso's sparsity directly reveals which features actually matter.
  • Prefer Ridge when you believe most features carry at least some small-but-real signal (rather than being pure noise), especially under multicollinearity - Ridge's smooth shrinkage stabilizes such coefficients without discarding any of them, whereas Lasso can somewhat arbitrarily pick just ONE of several correlated-but-genuinely-relevant features to keep and zero out the rest.
  • When correlated features are all individually meaningful and you don't want Lasso's sometimes-arbitrary "pick one, drop the others" behavior among them, or when you want a middle ground between shrinkage and sparsity, Elastic Net (combining L1 and L2 penalties) is often a more robust default choice.

Advantages

  • Built-in, automatic feature selection - as demonstrated, Lasso can reduce a wide feature set down to a compact, sparse model as an intrinsic part of training, with no separate feature-selection pipeline needed.
  • Produces more interpretable models on wide datasets - a model that assigns exactly zero to 180 out of 200 features is far easier to explain and reason about than one that assigns tiny but nonzero weight to all 200.
  • Reduces overfitting on high-dimensional data - by aggressively simplifying the model (fewer active features), Lasso often generalizes better than an unregularized model when the number of features is large relative to the number of samples.

Disadvantages / Limitations

  • Arbitrary selection among correlated features - when several features are highly correlated and all genuinely relevant, Lasso tends to pick one somewhat arbitrarily and zero out the others, which can discard useful signal and make the specific selected feature sensitive to noise in the training sample.
  • Has no closed-form solution - because the L1 penalty is not differentiable at zero, Lasso must be fit with an iterative optimization algorithm (such as coordinate descent, which scikit-learn uses internally) rather than a single matrix computation like OLS or Ridge.
  • Requires tuning alpha carefully - too small and Lasso barely differs from OLS (little to no sparsity); too large and it can zero out even genuinely important features, underfitting the data - again typically chosen via cross-validation.
codeExamples:
# Sweeping alpha to show increasingly aggressive feature elimination
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import Lasso

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, n_features = 150, 10
X = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, n_features))
true_beta = np.array([4.0, -3.0, 2.5, 0.1, 0.05, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0])  # only first 3 matter much
y = X @ true_beta + rng.normal(0, 0.3, n)

for alpha in [0.01, 0.1, 0.5, 1.0]:
    model = Lasso(alpha=alpha).fit(X, y)
    n_nonzero = np.sum(model.coef_ != 0)
    print(f"alpha={alpha:4.2f}  nonzero_features={n_nonzero:2d}  coefs={np.round(model.coef_, 2)}")
# OUTPUT (typical):
# alpha=0.01  nonzero_features=10  coefs=[ 3.98 -2.97  2.48  0.09  0.03 -0.01  0.02  0.   -0.01  0.  ]
# alpha=0.10  nonzero_features= 5  coefs=[ 3.9  -2.89  2.4   0.02  0.    0.    0.    0.    0.    0.  ]
# alpha=0.50  nonzero_features= 3  coefs=[ 3.53 -2.51  2.03  0.    0.    0.    0.    0.    0.    0.  ]
# alpha=1.00  nonzero_features= 3  coefs=[ 3.03 -2.02  1.53  0.    0.    0.    0.    0.    0.    0.  ]   <- exactly
#                                                                                the 3 truly important features
codeExplanations: Only the first three of ten features have a substantial true effect on y; the rest are either near-zero or exactly zero in truth. As alpha increases from 0.01 to 1.0, the number of nonzero coefficients Lasso keeps shrinks from all 10 down to exactly 3 - and those 3 are precisely the genuinely important features. This progression makes visible exactly how the alpha hyperparameter controls sparsity: small alpha barely regularizes at all (nearly every feature stays, however faintly), while large alpha aggressively prunes down to only the features whose real effect on the target is strong enough to outweigh the penalty for keeping them nonzero.

QuestionAnswer
What penalty does Lasso Regression add to the cost function, and how does it differ from Ridge's penalty?Lasso adds an L1 penalty, alpha times the sum of the ABSOLUTE VALUES of the coefficients, whereas Ridge adds an L2 penalty based on the sum of SQUARED coefficients; both discourage large coefficients, but only Lasso's L1 penalty can drive some coefficients to exactly zero
Why does Lasso's L1 penalty tend to produce exactly-zero coefficients while Ridge's L2 penalty does not?Geometrically, the L1 penalty region in coefficient space is a diamond/cross-polytope with sharp corners lying exactly on the coordinate axes (where one or more coefficients are zero); the smooth error contours are much more likely to first touch this region at one of those corners, forcing some coefficients to exactly zero, whereas the L2 penalty's smooth circular/spherical region generically touches the error contours at a point where all coefficients remain nonzero
When would you choose Lasso over Ridge, and when would you choose Ridge over Lasso?Choose Lasso when you suspect many of your features are irrelevant or redundant and want the model to automatically perform feature selection during training; choose Ridge when you believe most features carry at least some small-but-real signal, especially under multicollinearity, since Ridge stabilizes correlated coefficients without arbitrarily discarding some of them the way Lasso can

beginner.content:
Splitting the Difference Between Ridge and Lasso

Elastic Net is a linear regression model that combines BOTH regularization penalties you might already know separately - Ridge's L2 penalty (shrinks coefficients toward zero, keeps correlated features together) and Lasso's L1 penalty (can shrink coefficients all the way to exactly zero, performing automatic feature selection).
  • A mixing parameter called l1_ratio (between 0 and 1) controls the blend: l1_ratio=1 is pure Lasso, l1_ratio=0 is pure Ridge, and anything in between is a genuine combination of both effects.
  • A second parameter, alpha, controls the overall STRENGTH of the combined penalty, just like it does in Ridge and Lasso individually.
  • Elastic Net exists because Ridge and Lasso each have a specific weakness - Ridge never zeroes out useless features, while Lasso behaves erratically when features are highly correlated with each other (picking one at random from a correlated group and zeroing the rest) - and Elastic Net's blend fixes both at once.
codeExamples:
from sklearn.linear_model import ElasticNet, Ridge, Lasso
from sklearn.datasets import make_regression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error

X, y = make_regression(n_samples=200, n_features=10, n_informative=5, noise=15, random_state=0)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)

ridge = Ridge(alpha=1.0).fit(X_train, y_train)
lasso = Lasso(alpha=1.0).fit(X_train, y_train)
elastic = ElasticNet(alpha=1.0, l1_ratio=0.5).fit(X_train, y_train)

for name, model in [("Ridge", ridge), ("Lasso", lasso), ("Elastic Net", elastic)]:
    mse = mean_squared_error(y_test, model.predict(X_test))
    zero_coefs = sum(1 for c in model.coef_ if abs(c) < 1e-6)
    print(f"{name:12s} test MSE={mse:8.2f}  zeroed-out coefficients={zero_coefs}")
# OUTPUT (typical):
# Ridge        test MSE=  245.10  zeroed-out coefficients=0
# Lasso        test MSE=  268.40  zeroed-out coefficients=3
# Elastic Net  test MSE=  251.80  zeroed-out coefficients=2
codeExplanations: A synthetic regression dataset with 10 features, only 5 of which are actually informative, is split into train/test sets. Ridge, Lasso, and ElasticNet (with l1_ratio=0.5, an even blend) are each fit on the same training data. Printing test MSE alongside how many coefficients each model drove to exactly zero shows the tradeoff concretely: Ridge keeps every feature (zero coefficients dropped) since its L2 penalty only shrinks, Lasso aggressively zeroes out several coefficients via its L1 penalty, and Elastic Net lands in between - some feature selection happens, but less aggressively and less erratically than pure Lasso, which is exactly the middle-ground behavior l1_ratio is designed to produce.

expert.content:
Why This Matters

Before Elastic Net, practitioners regularizing a linear model had to commit to one of two penalties, each with a real cost. Ridge (L2) shrinks all coefficients smoothly toward zero but essentially never sets any of them to EXACTLY zero, so it never simplifies the model or tells you which features are truly irrelevant. Lasso (L1) can zero out coefficients entirely, which is great for feature selection - but when several features are highly CORRELATED with each other (measuring almost the same underlying thing), Lasso tends to arbitrarily pick just one of them to keep and zero out the rest, and which one it picks can change unpredictably with small changes in the data.
  • Elastic Net's combined L1 + L2 penalty inherits Lasso's ability to zero out genuinely useless features while inheriting Ridge's tendency to keep CORRELATED useful features together instead of arbitrarily discarding all but one.
  • This matters most whenever your feature set has groups of correlated variables - which is extremely common in real data (multiple sensors measuring similar things, multiple financial ratios derived from the same underlying numbers, or genes that tend to be expressed together).

Real-World Example

A genomics research team is building a model to predict a disease outcome from a patient's gene expression profile, where the dataset has THOUSANDS of gene features, many of which are highly correlated because genes in the same biological pathway tend to switch on and off together. Using pure Lasso here is dangerous: for each correlated GROUP of pathway genes, Lasso will typically keep just one arbitrary gene from the group and zero out the rest, even though biologically the whole group is relevant - and a different random train/test split could cause Lasso to keep a completely DIFFERENT gene from the same group, making the "important genes" list unstable and scientifically misleading. Elastic Net's Ridge component encourages correlated genes in the same pathway to receive similar, non-zero coefficients together, while its Lasso component still zeroes out entire pathways that truly have no relationship to the outcome - giving researchers a stable, biologically coherent set of relevant genes instead of an arbitrary single representative per pathway.
codeExamples:
# Simulating genomics-style correlated feature groups: Lasso's instability vs Elastic Net's grouping
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import Lasso, ElasticNet

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n_samples = 150

# Simulate a "pathway": 4 genes that are almost identical (highly correlated) and truly relevant
pathway_signal = rng.normal(0, 1, n_samples)
gene_group = np.column_stack([pathway_signal + rng.normal(0, 0.05, n_samples) for _ in range(4)])
# 6 unrelated, irrelevant genes (pure noise)
noise_genes = rng.normal(0, 1, (n_samples, 6))
X = np.column_stack([gene_group, noise_genes])
y = 5 * pathway_signal + rng.normal(0, 1, n_samples)  # outcome truly depends on the whole pathway

lasso = Lasso(alpha=0.5).fit(X, y)
elastic = ElasticNet(alpha=0.5, l1_ratio=0.5).fit(X, y)

print("Lasso coefficients on the 4 correlated pathway genes:      ", np.round(lasso.coef_[:4], 2))
print("Elastic Net coefficients on the 4 correlated pathway genes:", np.round(elastic.coef_[:4], 2))
# OUTPUT (typical):
# Lasso coefficients on the 4 correlated pathway genes:       [4.6  0.   0.   0. ]   <- arbitrarily kept only 1
# Elastic Net coefficients on the 4 correlated pathway genes: [1.2  1.1  1.3  1.2]   <- kept the whole group
codeExplanations: This builds a synthetic stand-in for the genomics scenario: 4 "pathway genes" that are nearly identical to each other (highly correlated) and genuinely drive the outcome, plus 6 unrelated noise genes. Lasso and Elastic Net are both fit on this data with comparable overall regularization strength. Printing each model's coefficients on just the 4 correlated pathway genes shows the exact failure mode described above: Lasso assigns almost all the weight to a single arbitrarily-chosen gene from the group and zeroes out the other three identical signals, while Elastic Net spreads the weight roughly evenly across all four - correctly reflecting that the whole correlated group matters, not just one arbitrary member of it.

expert.content:
Advantages

  • Handles correlated features far better than Lasso alone - as shown above, its Ridge component keeps correlated groups together instead of arbitrarily discarding all but one member, which is critical whenever features aren't cleanly independent.
  • Still performs automatic feature selection - unlike pure Ridge, it can drive genuinely irrelevant coefficients all the way to zero, producing a simpler, more interpretable model than Ridge would.
  • A safe default when you're unsure whether Ridge or Lasso is the better fit - rather than having to guess or run both separately, tuning l1_ratio (alongside alpha) via cross-validation lets the data itself decide how much of each penalty is appropriate, with l1_ratio values of 0 or 1 recovering pure Ridge or pure Lasso as special cases anyway.
  • More stable coefficient estimates across resampled datasets - because it doesn't make the same all-or-nothing, easily-flipped choices among correlated features that pure Lasso does, retraining on a slightly different sample tends to produce a similar set of selected features rather than a different arbitrary subset.

Disadvantages / Limitations

  • Two hyperparameters to tune instead of one - both alpha (overall strength) and l1_ratio (blend) need to be searched, typically via cross-validation (e.g. ElasticNetCV), which is more expensive than tuning Ridge or Lasso's single alpha alone.
  • Loses some of Lasso's sparsity - because part of the penalty is always L2, Elastic Net with a moderate l1_ratio typically keeps more nonzero coefficients than pure Lasso would at the same overall strength, which can be a downside if maximal sparsity/simplicity is the actual goal.
  • Still assumes an underlying linear relationship - like Ridge and Lasso, Elastic Net only regularizes a LINEAR model's coefficients; it does nothing to help if the true relationship between features and target is fundamentally nonlinear.
  • Requires feature scaling - since both L1 and L2 penalties are sensitive to the scale of each feature (a feature measured in the thousands would be penalized very differently from one measured in fractions), features must be standardized before fitting, or the penalty will be applied unevenly and unfairly across features.
codeExamples:
# Using ElasticNetCV to let cross-validation pick both alpha and l1_ratio automatically
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import ElasticNetCV
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.datasets import make_regression

X, y = make_regression(n_samples=300, n_features=20, n_informative=8, noise=10, random_state=1)

model = make_pipeline(
    StandardScaler(),
    ElasticNetCV(l1_ratio=[0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 1.0], alphas=np.logspace(-2, 1, 20), cv=5)
)
model.fit(X, y)

enet = model.named_steps["elasticnetcv"]
print(f"Best alpha found:    {enet.alpha_:.4f}")
print(f"Best l1_ratio found: {enet.l1_ratio_:.2f}")
print(f"Nonzero coefficients: {sum(1 for c in enet.coef_ if abs(c) > 1e-6)} out of {len(enet.coef_)}")
# OUTPUT (typical):
# Best alpha found:    0.0480
# Best l1_ratio found: 0.70
# Nonzero coefficients: 9 out of 20
codeExplanations: Rather than guessing alpha and l1_ratio by hand, ElasticNetCV performs 5-fold cross-validation over a grid of candidate l1_ratio values and a range of alpha values (generated on a log scale via np.logspace), selecting whichever combination minimizes cross-validated error - the features are standardized first via StandardScaler inside a pipeline, since both penalties are scale-sensitive. The fitted model's alpha_ and l1_ratio_ attributes report the winning combination, and counting nonzero coefficients shows that, on this dataset (20 features, 8 truly informative), the cross-validated Elastic Net settled on a fairly Lasso-leaning blend (l1_ratio around 0.7) that keeps roughly the right number of features rather than all 20 or an overly sparse handful.
